prompt: After his family left West Philadelphia, where did Walter E. Williams spend much of his childhood?

choices.text: Chicago’s Cabrini-Green
North Philadelphia’s Richard Allen housing projects
Harlem’s Lenox Terrace
Atlanta’s Techwood Homes

explain: Williams was born in Philadelphia in 1936. His father was not part of raising him. The family later moved to the Richard Allen projects. He tells that story in his autobiography.
source: Walter E. Williams, “Law vs. Moral Values” (2009), http://walterewilliams.com/law-vs.-moral-values/ . The column places his 1940s childhood in North Philadelphia’s Richard Allen housing project.

prompt: Where did Williams earn his economics PhD, and what was the dissertation?

choices.text: The University of Chicago in 1968. The dissertation is Capitalism and Freedom
Harvard in 1975. The dissertation is The Affluent Society
UCLA in 1972. The dissertation is The Low-Income Market Place
George Mason in 1980. The dissertation is The State Against Blacks

explain: He took a BA in economics from California State College at Los Angeles in 1965, then an MA and a PhD from UCLA. George Mason is where he later taught. The State Against Blacks is a 1982 book, not the dissertation.
source: UCLA Economics memorial; about page on walterewilliams.com

prompt: Which post did Williams hold from 1980 until his death?

choices.text: Hoover Institution senior fellow who never taught undergraduates
Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under Reagan
Tenured professor at Temple University for the whole period after 1980
John M. Olin Distinguished Professor of Economics at George Mason University, and department chair from 1995 to 2001

explain: He taught at Temple before 1980, then joined George Mason in 1980 and chaired economics there from 1995 to 2001. He kept teaching at George Mason through his last class in 2020. His own sketch names the post John M. Olin Distinguished Professor of Economics, held since 1980, with the chairmanship from 1995 to 2001, and lists earlier faculties at Los Angeles City College, California State University Los Angeles, Temple, and Grove City College. Dean Ann Ardis's [December 2, 2020 statement](https://chss.gmu.edu/articles/15237) says he was 84, still the John M. Olin Distinguished Professor, on the faculty for four decades, and chairman of Economics from 1995 to 2001. Hoover's December 8, 2020 notice places that chair in Fairfax, Virginia.
source: Ann Ardis, "Appreciation for Dr. Walter Williams," George Mason University College of Humanities and Social Sciences, December 2, 2020, https://chss.gmu.edu/articles/15237

prompt: Which claim does The State Against Blacks argue most directly?

choices.text: Government rules such as minimum wages, occupational licensing, and entry limits have often blocked Black economic progress
Private markets are the main barrier to Black employment, so licensing should expand
Discrimination is impossible once a law mentions race
Only federal jobs programs can raise Black incomes

explain: The book treats the state as a barrier to Black economic progress. Chapters cover the minimum wage, taxicab medallions, and licensing in trades such as plumbing.
source: The State Against Blacks (McGraw-Hill, 1982). Michael Novak, Commentary, 1 April 1983, summarizes the minimum-wage, taxicab, and licensing chapters, https://www.commentary.org/articles/michael-novak-2/the-state-against-blacks-by-walter-e-williams/

prompt: In Williams’s minimum-wage argument, what happens when the law requires a wage above what a worker’s hourly output is worth to the employer?

choices.text: Employers hire more of those workers because the wage is now fair
Output rises on its own to match the legal wage
Hiring that worker becomes a loss, so the job often disappears
The wage floor creates a surplus of vacancies for the least skilled

explain: He asks the employer’s question. If you must pay a legal minimum to anyone you hire, you do not hire someone who produces less than that per hour. He treats the result as unemployment for the least skilled. In the August 31, 2011 column [Race and Economics](http://walterewilliams.com/race-and-economics/), he sets the legal wage at $7.25 and the worker’s hourly output at $4, and he calls that hire a losing proposition. The column prints overall unemployment at 9.1 percent, white adults at 8 percent, white teens at 23 percent, black adults at 17 percent, and black teens at 40 percent, more than 50 percent in some cities, Washington among them.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Race and Economics," walterewilliams.com, August 31, 2011, http://walterewilliams.com/race-and-economics/

prompt: What does Williams argue about the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931?

choices.text: It abolished union wages so Black contractors could underbid anyone
It applied only to farms and never mentioned construction
He treats it as a minor rule with no labor-market effect
Its prevailing-wage rule on federal construction was debated in terms that targeted lower-paid Black labor, and he says Black workers then largely left those projects

explain: In his columns he points to the legislative debate, including members of Congress and the AFL president objecting to Southern contractors who used lower-paid Black workers. He argues the law then shut those workers out of federal construction. Outside research. Williams's column [Race and Economics](http://walterewilliams.com/race-and-economics/), 31 August 2011, quotes Rep. John Cochran on "Southern contractors employing low-paid colored mechanics," Rep. Clayton Allgood on "cheap colored labor," and AFL president William Green, then says black workers on federal construction "virtually disappeared" for decades. David Bernstein, Cato Briefing Paper No. 17, 1993, [The Davis-Bacon Act: Let's Bring Jim Crow to an End](https://www.cato.org/briefing-paper/davis-bacon-act-lets-bring-jim-crow-end), prints the Allgood remark with its citation, Congressional Record, 28 February 1931, page 6513, and Green's testimony to the Senate Committee on Manufactures, 3 February 1931. The exclusion claim rests on the histories Bernstein cites, not on an employment series. Kessler and Katz, [NBER Working Paper 7454](https://www.nber.org/papers/w7454), find that repeal of state prevailing-wage laws in 1970 to 1993 narrowed the black and nonblack construction wage gap, which is later evidence on related state laws, not on the 1931 act.
source: Columns “Race and Economics” and “Minimum Wage and Discrimination” on walterewilliams.com

prompt: Which claim is closest to the thesis of South Africa’s War Against Capitalism?

choices.text: Free markets created apartheid and needed more central planning to undo it
Apartheid, including job-reservation laws, worked against market pressures that would have put Black workers into jobs reserved for whites
Job-reservation laws were unnecessary because no white employer would hire a Black worker
The book defends apartheid as a capitalist policy

explain: Williams argues apartheid was not a product of free markets. Job-reservation laws existed, in his account, because some employers would have hired Black workers at lower wages. He says racists could not trust markets to keep the color bar. Outside research. Matthew Kibbe's 1990 Freeman review, [South Africa's War Against Capitalism](https://fee.org/articles/book-review-south-africas-war-against-capitalism-by-walter-e-williams/), quotes the book: "The presence of job reservation laws suggests that at least some employers would hire blacks in the 'white jobs,'" and "This is why South African white workers resorted to government." The laws are real. South African History Online, [Apartheid Legislation 1850s-1970s](https://sahistory.org.za/article/apartheid-legislation-1850s-1970s), describes the Mines and Works Act of 1911 and the 1926 Colour Bar Act as reserving skilled mine work for whites after mine owners kept moving work to lower-paid Black miners. The O'Malley Archives [chronology of apartheid legislation](https://omalley.nelsonmandela.org/index.php/site/q/03lv02167/04lv02264/05lv02335/06lv02357/07lv02359/08lv02371.htm) records section 77 of the Industrial Conciliation Act of 1956 as the job-reservation provision.
source: South Africa’s War Against Capitalism (Praeger, 1989); column “Discrimination and Segregation” on walterewilliams.com

prompt: A city caps rents far below the market to create “affordable” housing. Which reaction matches Williams?

choices.text: Expect a shortage, and a market that stays costly for people who cannot get a controlled unit. He makes the same point about 1970s gasoline price controls
Expect builders to add apartments because the cap makes tenants richer
Treat the shortage as proof the cap was set too high
Conclude that housing demand does not respond to price

explain: In "Compassion Versus Reality" he says rent controls aimed at affordable housing, and price controls aimed at price-gouging, produce a calamity worse than the original problem. He names San Francisco and New York as costly rent-controlled markets and recalls the chaos of 1970s gasoline price controls. "Gas Prices and Price Controls" says those controls caused shortages and long lines. Outside research. The column is [Compassion Versus Reality](https://www.creators.com/read/walter-williams/06/07/compassion-versus-reality), June 2007. Diamond, McQuade, and Qian, [NBER Working Paper 24181](https://www.nber.org/papers/w24181), find that San Francisco landlords brought under rent control in 1994 cut rental supply by 15 percent, and the working paper puts the citywide rent increase at 5.1 percent. Glaeser and Luttmer, [American Economic Review, 2003](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/000282803769206188), find a significant share of New York apartments misallocated under rent control. A 1995 National Petroleum Council report hosted by the [Department of Energy](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2022-11/eo1995-Future_Issues-View_of_US_Oil_n_Natural_Gas_to_2020.pdf) says the 1973 embargo "combined with federal price and allocation controls" to produce the gasoline lines, and that 1979 brought more.
source: “Compassion Versus Reality,” http://walterewilliams.com/compassion-versus-reality/ ; “Gas Prices and Price Controls,” Capitalism Magazine, 7 December 2005, https://capitalismmagazine.com/2005/12/gas-prices-and-price-controls/

prompt: After a demand spike, a legislature freezes the price of flour below the market. Which pattern does Williams’s price-control lesson predict?

choices.text: Farmers plant more because the freeze guarantees them a loss
Shortages prove the ceiling was above the market price
Millers and farmers have less reason to expand output, so flour runs short and black markets appear
A legal ceiling raises the quantity supplied

explain: In Economics for the Citizen he uses a flour ceiling as the example. If the controlled price does not pay for extra output, suppliers do not expand, and people trade at illegal prices. Outside research. The passage is in [Economics for the Citizen: Part V](https://fee.org/articles/economics-for-the-citizen-part-v/) at FEE. "Would wheat farmers put more land under cultivation? Would millers work overtime to produce more flour? The answer is a big fat no because what would be in it for them?" He then predicts flour shortages and black markets. The Freeman printed the series in five parts. The ten-part syndicated version has different numbering, and its Part 5 does not contain the flour example.
source: Economics for the Citizen, Part V, FEE, 1 August 2006, https://fee.org/articles/economics-for-the-citizen-part-v/ . Capitalism Magazine prints that flour essay as Part 9, 20 January 2005, https://capitalismmagazine.com/2005/01/economics-for-the-citizen-part-9/ . Its Part 5 is a different essay.

prompt: A city requires an expensive taxi medallion before anyone can drive a cab. A poor person owns a used car and wants to start. What is Williams’s licensing argument?

choices.text: The high price means more poor people will enter, because the license is a status good
Occupational licensing raises employment for the least skilled
Only safety rules matter, so entry limits have no income pattern
The medallion blocks a bottom rung that used to be open. He contrasts an earlier New York, where a used car was enough, with later medallion prices that shut poor entrants out

explain: The State Against Blacks treats taxicab licensing in New York, Philadelphia, and Washington as an entry barrier. Michael Novak's April 1983 review reports his contrast. In the 1920s a poor person could start with a used car. By the time of the book, a New York license cost about $60,000. Outside research. The review is [The State Against Blacks, by Walter E. Williams](https://www.commentary.org/articles/michael-novak-2/the-state-against-blacks-by-walter-e-williams/) in Commentary. Bruce Schaller's [New York City Taxicab Fact Book](https://www.schallerconsult.com/taxi/taxifb.pdf), Table 4, puts the average individual medallion at $60,000 in 1980 and 1981 and $57,500 in 1982. A 1986 [Transportation Research Record paper](https://onlinepubs.trb.org/Onlinepubs/trr/1986/1103/1103-010.pdf) reports $50,000 to $60,000 in 1981. The 1937 Haas Act froze the license count at 13,595, per Schaller's history page, [NY's Taxi Medallion System](https://www.schallerconsult.com/taxi/taxi2.htm). Before 1937 there were no medallions, and Schaller records 21,000 cabs on the street by 1931 under open entry.
source: The State Against Blacks, taxicab chapters; Michael Novak, Commentary, 1 April 1983, https://www.commentary.org/articles/michael-novak-2/the-state-against-blacks-by-walter-e-williams/

prompt: A council raises the wage floor above what many teenagers can produce in an hour, and says the law will help them. Which follow-up matches Williams?

choices.text: Ask only whether the council meant well
Ask which teenagers an employer will still hire once their output is worth less than the mandated wage
Assume employment of the least skilled rises one-for-one with the wage
Treat a later drop in teen jobs as proof the wage was set too low

explain: He separates intention from effect. A higher floor, in his account, makes it a loss to hire a worker who produces less than the legal wage per hour. He argues the harm lands hardest on low-skilled teenagers. The March 23, 2005 column [Minimum wage, maximum folly](https://www.wnd.com/2005/03/29486/) asks what a policy’s effects are, not its intentions, and it puts the wage at $6.25 or $7.25 an hour against a worker who produces only $4 of value. It says teenagers dominate that low-skilled group. Bureau of Labor Statistics figures in the column put teen unemployment at 16 percent for whites and 32 percent for blacks, against 1948 rates of 9.4 percent for black teens ages 16 to 17 and 10.2 percent for white teens. A 40-cent minimum in force before 1948 had been essentially repealed by postwar inflation, the column says, and later increases left black teen unemployment permanently double the white teen rate. It adds that only 2.2 percent of working adults earn the minimum.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Minimum wage, maximum folly," WorldNetDaily, March 23, 2005, https://www.wnd.com/2005/03/29486/

prompt: Group A earns more than Group B. An advocate says the gap itself proves discrimination and nothing else. Which reply is closest to Williams?

choices.text: A gap proves that markets have already erased every legal barrier
Discrimination has never existed, so stop counting incomes
A gap has many possible causes. His 2011 book asks how much can be blamed on discrimination, and he also asks which laws price out the least skilled
Only genetics can explain a gap, so ignore law and skills

explain: Race and Economics: How Much Can Be Blamed on Discrimination? refuses the leap from unequal outcomes to one cause. The State Against Blacks adds a second question. Which rules cut the jobs and licenses the least skilled could have used? The August 31, 2011 column [Race and Economics](http://walterewilliams.com/race-and-economics/) quotes chapter 3 of that book: during gross racial discrimination, black unemployment was lower and blacks were more active in the labor force than today. It prints 1910 employment of 71 percent for black males older than 9, against 51 percent for whites, and it says that as early as 1890 the duration of unemployment was shorter among blacks than among whites. Discrimination or low skills, he writes, can explain low wages but not unemployment. The rules he names on that page are the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931, after which black workers on federally financed or assisted construction virtually disappeared, then the National Industrial Recovery Act of 1933 and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. In the Davis-Bacon debate the column quotes Rep. Clayton Allgood on “cheap colored labor” and AFL president William Green saying colored labor was being sought to demoralize wage rates.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Race and Economics," walterewilliams.com, August 31, 2011, http://walterewilliams.com/race-and-economics/

prompt: A government bans Black workers from skilled mine jobs and says employers would never have hired them anyway. What question does Williams ask?

choices.text: The ban proves markets want racial job reservation
A lower wage offer is too minor to discuss, so the law changed nothing
Job reservation is what free entry looks like
If employers already refused, why was a law required? He argues some would have hired Black workers at a lower wage, so the color bar needed the state

explain: In "Discrimination and Segregation" he notes South African job-reservation laws for work such as running elevators and supervising machinery. He argues racists cannot trust free markets to keep those jobs white. Outside research. The column is [Discrimination and Segregation](https://www.creators.com/read/walter-williams/10/16/discrimination-and-segregation), 5 October 2016, and its list is blasting, running elevators, driving engines, supervising boilers and other machinery, supervising shifts, and overseeing mines. The mining bar is the Mines and Works Act of 1911 and its 1926 amendment, which South African History Online, [Apartheid Legislation 1850s-1970s](https://sahistory.org.za/article/apartheid-legislation-1850s-1970s), describes as limiting certificates of competency for skilled mining occupations to whites and Coloureds. Elevators were also reserved by name outside the mines. Determination No. 5 under section 77 of the Industrial Conciliation Act of 1956 reserved passenger lift attendants in Johannesburg, Pretoria, and Bloemfontein for whites from 1963 to 1977, as cited by Mariotti and van Zyl-Hermann, [Economic History of Developing Regions, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1080/20780389.2014.955273), and described in a [Stellenbosch seminar report on Bridget Kenny's research](https://www.stias.ac.za/public-lectures-seminars/how-to-fix-a-lift-the-political-intimacies-of-elevators-in-20th-century-johannesburg/).
source: Column “Discrimination and Segregation”; South Africa’s War Against Capitalism

prompt: Supporters of a new licensing exam say it protects the public. The written section is unrelated to the work, and people who pass the practical test still fail it. What would Williams stress?

choices.text: A written test that people fail is proof the trade is safer
Effect can diverge from intention. An entry exam can screen out competent poor and minority applicants even when the stated goal is safety
Intention is the only result that matters
Licensing always increases the number of practitioners

explain: Reviewers of The State Against Blacks describe his Missouri beautician example. Applicants faced a written portion and a performance portion. The written portion, not the practical one, drove a racial gap in who passed. His point is the effect of the rule. Outside research. Susan Love Brown's June 1983 review, [Government the Problem, Not the Panacea](https://reason.com/1983/06/01/government-the-problem-not-the/), gives his figures. Blacks were 3 percent of those who passed and 21 percent of those who failed, scored about 10 points lower on the written test at comparable education, and showed no significant difference on the performance test. Williams's 1980 Imprimis essay, [The Poor as First Victims of the Welfare State](https://www.northwood.edu/news/timeless-values-the-poor-as-first-victims-of-the-welfare-state/), names the study as Stuart Dorsey's work on Missouri and Illinois cosmetology exams, with a practical pass rate near 96 percent for everyone. Dorsey's published version is [The Occupational Licensing Queue](https://www.jstor.org/stable/145292), Journal of Human Resources, 1980, which this pass could not read.
source: The State Against Blacks, occupational licensing; Reason, June 1983, summarizes the Missouri beautician exam

prompt: When and where was Walter E. Williams born?

choices.text: March 31, 1936, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
July 4, 1930, in Atlanta, Georgia
January 15, 1929, in Chicago, Illinois
November 22, 1942, in Richmond, Virginia

explain: He was born in Philadelphia on March 31, 1936. Notices of his death give his age as 84, which matches that year. His own biographical sketch names Philadelphia and does not give the calendar date. The BlackPast profile prints the day: born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on March 31, 1936. Hoover's December 8, 2020 notice says he was born in 1936 to humble origins in Philadelphia and died on Tuesday, December 1, at 84, and does not print March 31. [BlackPast profile](https://blackpast.org/african-american-history/williams-walter-edward-1936/).
source: Elwood Watson, "Walter Edward Williams (1936-2020)," BlackPast, October 28, 2013, https://blackpast.org/african-american-history/williams-walter-edward-1936/

prompt: Who was in the household that raised Williams?

choices.text: Both parents, in a two-parent home for his whole childhood
His grandparents, after both parents moved to Los Angeles
His mother and his sister. His father played no role in raising them.
A foster family. He had no siblings.

explain: The household was his mother, his sister, and him. His father was not part of raising them. They lived first in West Philadelphia and later in the Richard Allen projects. David Henderson's Hoover account says Walter and his sister were raised by their mother in a government housing project in North Philadelphia, and that his father had left when Walter was two or three. Hoover's book page for Up from the Projects places the early years in a mixed but predominantly black neighborhood in West Philadelphia. The February 5, 2021 profile says he grew up in the housing projects of Philadelphia with a single mother. [Appreciating Walter Williams](https://www.hoover.org/research/appreciating-walter-williams).
source: David R. Henderson, "Appreciating Walter Williams," Defining Ideas, Hoover Institution, January 22, 2021, https://www.hoover.org/research/appreciating-walter-williams

prompt: Which account matches his military service?

choices.text: He enlisted in the Navy in 1948 and stayed in Philadelphia for the whole enlistment.
He was drafted in 1959 into the U.S. Army and was later transferred to South Korea.
A student deferment kept him out of service through his UCLA doctorate.
He was an Army officer in West Germany from 1973 to 1980, while he taught at Temple.

explain: After high school and a stretch driving a cab in Philadelphia, he was drafted in 1959. While in the service he was transferred to South Korea. He wrote that in 1959, before the draft, he drove for Yellow Cab in Philadelphia for about $400 a month, and that in August he was earning a recruit's $68 a month. Basic training was at Fort Jackson, South Carolina, and he was then stationed at Fort Stewart, Georgia, where he was court-martialed and won. In 1960 he was in Incheon, South Korea. David Henderson's [Hoover account](https://www.hoover.org/research/appreciating-walter-williams) calls him an Army draftee from 1959 to 1961 in Georgia and South Korea.
source: David R. Henderson, "Appreciating Walter Williams," Defining Ideas, Hoover Institution, January 22, 2021, https://www.hoover.org/research/appreciating-walter-williams

prompt: What do the memorial accounts agree on about his death?

choices.text: He retired when the chairmanship ended in 2001 and died in Philadelphia in 2010.
He left George Mason in 1995 for a daily television show and died in 2017, the year of the Bradley Prize.
He died in 1989 while in South Africa researching his book on apartheid.
He died in 2020 at age 84, shortly after teaching a class at George Mason University.

explain: Hoover's 2021 profile dates his death December 1, 2020. A Wall Street Journal tribute quoted by UCLA says he died the morning after teaching his final class, at 84. Those notices do not use the same calendar day, so the shared facts are the year, his age, and that he had just taught at George Mason. Outside research. Hoover's [profile](https://www.hoover.org/news/walter-williams) and its [8 December 2020 notice](https://www.hoover.org/news/walter-e-williams-1936-2020) say Tuesday, December 1. [UCLA Economics](https://economics.ucla.edu/walter-williams-ucla-ph-d/) quotes the Journal: "died Wednesday morning after teaching his final class at George Mason University on Tuesday." The Washington Post gives December 2 and quotes a university spokesman that his class ended at 10 p.m. on December 1. The New York Times gives Tuesday and reports his daughter's account that he died in his car after teaching. George Mason's own [dean's statement](https://chss.gmu.edu/articles/15237) gives no date. The Times and the Post both give his birth date as March 31, 1936.
source: Hoover Institution, "Black History Month Profile: Walter Williams" (February 5, 2021); UCLA Economics memorial quoting Donald J. Boudreaux, Wall Street Journal

prompt: What is the documented account of his marriage?

choices.text: He married Connie Taylor in 1960. She died in 2007. They had one daughter.
He married in 1980, the year he joined George Mason, and had no children.
Connie in the obituaries is his sister. He did not marry.
He married Constance Sowell in 1972, the year of his PhD.

explain: He married Connie Taylor in 1960. She died in 2007. They had one daughter. Hoover's December 8, 2020 notice prints the marriage: Connie (née Taylor), from 1960 until she passed away in 2007, and names their daughter Devon. A BlackPast profile opened for this pass says she died in 2009, which is the later conflict the 2007 notice does not share. [Hoover notice](https://www.hoover.org/news/walter-e-williams-1936-2020).
source: Hoover Institution, "Walter E. Williams, 1936–2020," December 8, 2020, https://www.hoover.org/news/walter-e-williams-1936-2020

prompt: Which high school did Williams graduate from?

choices.text: Central High School in Philadelphia
Benjamin Franklin High School in North Philadelphia
Dunbar High School in Washington, D.C.
Los Angeles High School

explain: He attended and graduated from Benjamin Franklin High School in North Philadelphia. Dunbar High School is a school he later wrote about. It is not the school he attended. In "Declining standards" he writes that he attended Philadelphia's Benjamin Franklin High School, graduating in 1954, when it was a predominantly black school for the city's poorest children, with mostly white teachers and, by his recollection, only two black teachers. That [column](http://walterewilliams.com/declining-standards/) does not print the words North Philadelphia, and the page has no dateline.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Declining standards," walterewilliams.com (opened page prints no dateline), http://walterewilliams.com/declining-standards/

prompt: What does Hoover's profile say pushed him toward economics as an undergraduate?

choices.text: A required course with Milton Friedman at Chicago
Thomas Sowell assigning The Wealth of Nations
Reading W. E. B. Du Bois's Black Reconstruction, and its argument that Black Americans needed to understand the economic system
A Bureau of Labor Statistics job that came with a scholarship

explain: The Hoover profile says he was inspired to study economics at California State University, Los Angeles, after reading Du Bois's Black Reconstruction. The February 5, 2021 [profile](https://www.hoover.org/news/walter-williams) says Du Bois, whom it calls an NAACP cofounder, argued that African Americans could advance only if they understood the nation's economic system. The same profile says that in high school he packed orders for Sears Roebuck and ran a sewing machine at a hat factory, and that a seamstress reported him under the child-labor law.
source: Hoover Institution, "Black History Month Profile: Walter Williams," February 5, 2021, https://www.hoover.org/news/walter-williams

prompt: What is the first lesson of Economics for the Citizen, and when did he start that series?

choices.text: The first lesson is that a higher minimum wage raises employment. He wrote the series as department chairman in 1995.
The first lesson is scarcity. Wants exceed the means to meet them. He started the series during a fall semester off after two terms as chairman.
The first lesson is that rent control increases construction. The series is his 1972 dissertation.
The series is a high-school textbook the Philadelphia schools adopted in 1960.

explain: In the May 2005 Freeman piece he says the semester off was his reward for two terms as chairman at George Mason, and that he used it to write basic lectures for general readers. The first lesson he states is scarcity. Outside research. The piece is [Economics for the Citizen](https://fee.org/articles/economics-for-the-citizen/) at FEE, and the Freeman scan with the May 2005 running head is [May05.pdf](http://walterewilliams.com/publications/freeman/May05.pdf). "For the first time in 37 years, last fall semester I didn't teach," he writes, and "The first lesson in economic theory is that we live in a world of scarcity." The same text ran first as a ten-part syndicated series in January 2005, starting with [Part 1 at Capitalism Magazine](https://capitalismmagazine.com/2005/01/economics-for-the-citizen-part-1/). Hoover and George Mason date his chairmanship to 1995 to 2001.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Economics for the Citizen," The Freeman, May 2005, posted at walterewilliams.com

prompt: A mayor says a larger school budget will make up for parents who do not get children to school ready to learn. Which reply matches "Is politics the way?"

choices.text: A high enough per-pupil budget can replace parenting.
The money works only if it is reserved for vocational tracks.
Spending more cannot replace parenting. Homework, sleep, breakfast, and getting to school on time are not jobs a president or a mayor can do.
He does not discuss schools in that column. It is only about taxi medallions.

explain: Spending more cannot replace parenting. Homework, sleep, breakfast, and getting to school on time are not jobs a president or a mayor can do. The column on his site says someone must make children do their homework, get a good night's rest, fix a breakfast, and get to school on time and obey school authorities, and asks whether a president, congressman, or mayor can do that. It answers, "Spending more money on education cannot replace poor parenting." The opened page prints no dateline. [Is politics the way?](http://walterewilliams.com/is-politics-the-way/).
source: Walter E. Williams, "Is politics the way?," walterewilliams.com (opened page prints no dateline), http://walterewilliams.com/is-politics-the-way/

prompt: What did he do at Los Angeles City College before his economics degrees?

choices.text: He earned his PhD there in 1965.
He attended for one semester after high school, then returned to Philadelphia.
He was the college president from 1967 to 1969.
He never enrolled. He went from the Army straight into the UCLA doctoral program.

explain: After high school he lived with his father in California and attended Los Angeles City College for one semester, then went back to Philadelphia. He later taught at that college. That teaching job is a different part of the story. The bachelor's degree is from California State College at Los Angeles in 1965.
source: Wikipedia, Early life and education, citing Up from the Projects, p. 28

prompt: Which study did the Joint Economic Committee print under his name in 1977?

choices.text: Youth and Minority Unemployment, on minimum wages, the Davis-Bacon Act, licensing, and related restrictions
A legislative history of the Davis-Bacon Act that he wrote as a congressional staffer in 1931
A report urging a higher federal minimum wage as the way to cut teen unemployment
The Low-Income Market Place, adopted by the committee as a statute

explain: The committee print of July 6, 1977 is Youth and Minority Unemployment, by Walter E. Williams. It reviews minimum wages, union rules, the Davis-Bacon Act, licensing, schooling, and manpower policy. Hoover's later profile ties the minimum-wage and Davis-Bacon research to his national fellowship there in the mid-1970s. The profile misspells the statute Davis-Beacon. The print uses Davis-Bacon. Outside research. The Joint Economic Committee hosts the [print as a PDF](https://www.jec.senate.gov/reports/95th%20Congress/Youth%20and%20Minority%20Unemployment%20%28842%29.pdf). The title page carries the date and print number 89-825, the author footnote places him at Temple University, and the contents list Minimum wage laws, Unions, The Davis-Bacon Act, Licensure, Education, and Effects of past manpower policies. ERIC catalogs it as [ED155250](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED155250). The Hoover profile is [Black History Month Profile: Walter Williams](https://www.hoover.org/news/walter-williams), which dates the fellowship to 1975 to 1976 and spells the act Davis-Beacon. Hoover Institution Press also issued a 1977 edition that his publications list calls an unexpurgated version of the committee report.
source: Joint Economic Committee print, Youth and Minority Unemployment, by Walter E. Williams (July 6, 1977); Hoover Institution profile, February 5, 2021

prompt: An employer must pay the same legal wage to every hire of equal productivity. Which follow-up is the one in "Discrimination and Liberty"?

choices.text: The law fines an employer who hires across racial lines, so race disappears from the choice.
With no wage difference left, indulging a racial preference costs less. His analogy is a law that forces chuck steak to sell at the filet price.
Payroll offices then sort applicants by race as a requirement of the statute.
He says employers ignore wages and hire only by statute.

explain: He argues that a mandated wage lowers the cost of preferring one worker over another of equal productivity. The filet-and-chuck example makes the same point without race. If both cuts must sell at the filet price, the cheaper cut loses the discount that had been its way in. The April 1, 1998 essay [Discrimination and Liberty](https://fee.org/articles/discrimination-and-liberty/) prices filet mignon at twelve dollars a pound and chuck steak at seven, so the cost of passing over chuck is five dollars a pound. A law requiring both to sell for twelve dollars would drop that cost to zero. The wage case on the same page is a minimum of five dollars an hour and ten equally productive applicants, of whom the employer hires six, so the remaining choice is non-economic and may be race.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Discrimination and Liberty," FEE, April 1, 1998, https://fee.org/articles/discrimination-and-liberty/

prompt: Besides a wage floor, what does that essay say subsidizes personal preferences?

choices.text: Only statutes that name a race. Taxes and licenses do not.
Government setting the terms of exchange, including taxes on profits, economic regulation, and occupational licensure
Private boycotts alone. He says government does not change the cost of a preference.
School vouchers, which he calls the main subsidy for discrimination in that essay

explain: The essay treats a minimum wage as one case of a wider pattern. Preferences get a subsidy whenever government dictates the terms of exchange. He names taxes on profits, economic regulation, and occupational licensure. [Discrimination and Liberty](https://fee.org/articles/discrimination-and-liberty/) states that list in one sentence: taxes on profits, economic regulation, and occupational licensure, and it says preferences are subsidized whenever government dictates the terms and conditions of exchange. The page does not print a tax rate or a license fee. The priced case it does give is a minimum of five dollars an hour, with ten equally productive applicants and six hires, so the criterion left can be race. It also quotes the 1918 Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen: where rates of pay do not differ, the restrictions on the percentage of Negroes to be employed do not apply.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Discrimination and Liberty," FEE, April 1, 1998, https://fee.org/articles/discrimination-and-liberty/

prompt: A commentator says every serious problem in black neighborhoods is still a civil-rights problem, so the remedy is another statute. What does "Is politics the way?" answer?

choices.text: Constitutional protections are still denied, so the next civil-rights statute is the remedy.
Family structure and crime are beside the point next to a new voting bill.
A president can make children do their homework, so the remedy is national.
The struggle over constitutional protections has been won. Discrimination has not vanished. The devastating problems he is discussing are not civil-rights problems, and politics will not solve them.

explain: The November 3, 2004 column says black Americans now have the constitutional protections others have. He does not claim every trace of discrimination is gone. He says the problems of family, schooling, and crime that the column discusses are not civil-rights problems. [Is politics the way?](http://walterewilliams.com/is-politics-the-way/) puts the share of black children in two-parent families at around 70 percent from 1880 to 1960, and at 85 percent in 1925 Harlem, against 38 percent when he wrote. It puts black illegitimacy at 16 percent in 1940 and 70 percent in the column. On schooling, he asks whether a president, congressman, or mayor can make a child do homework, sleep, eat breakfast, and get to school on time. On crime, he describes bars, roll-down gates, security guards, and high insurance on neighborhood stores. He adds that civil rights law and more than $8 trillion spent on poverty programs since 1965 did not solve those problems.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Is politics the way?," walterewilliams.com, November 3, 2004, http://walterewilliams.com/is-politics-the-way/

prompt: In "The Welfare State's Legacy," what comparison does he draw for black children in single-parent families?

choices.text: About 70 percent in 1960, falling to 22 percent fifty years later, which he credits to the Great Society
22 percent in 1960, and more than 70 percent fifty years later. He asks whether that rise is a legacy of slavery or of the welfare state.
No change from 1890 to 2017, so he treats family structure as irrelevant
The Census stopped counting family structure after 1954, so the comparison cannot be made

explain: The September 20, 2017 column says that in 1960, 22 percent of black children were raised in single-parent families, and that fifty years later the share was more than 70 percent. He poses the slavery-or-welfare-state question in those words. Outside research. The column is [The Welfare State's Legacy](https://www.creators.com/read/walter-williams/09/17/the-welfare-states-legacy). Census table CH-3, [ch3.xls](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/tables/families/time-series/children/ch3.xls), puts 1,897 of 8,650 thousand nonwhite children with one parent in 1960, which is 21.9 percent and matches his 22. The same table's 2010 row puts 53.3 percent of black children with one parent and 60.8 percent not living with two parents. Nothing in it reaches 70 percent. The figure that does is births. NCHS, [Births: Final Data for 2010](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr61/nvsr61_01.pdf), Table 15, reports 72.5 percent of births to non-Hispanic black mothers as births to unmarried women. His 1960 number is a living-arrangement share and his 2010 number matches a birth share.
source: Walter E. Williams, "The Welfare State's Legacy," walterewilliams.com, September 20, 2017

prompt: What does that 2017 column say about black labor-force activity from 1890 to 1954?

choices.text: In every census in that span, blacks were as active as whites or more active, and black teen unemployment was about equal to or lower than white teen unemployment.
Blacks were left out of labor-force statistics until the Civil Rights Act.
Black teen unemployment was about double the white rate in each of those censuses.
He says usable data start in 1965, so earlier decades are out of reach.

explain: He uses those census years to ask whether anyone would claim racial discrimination was lighter then. His explanation for the later pattern is labor rules that cut off the bottom rungs. Outside research. The column is [The Welfare State's Legacy](https://www.creators.com/read/walter-williams/09/17/the-welfare-states-legacy). Historical Statistics of the United States, Series D 42-48 in [Chapter D](https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/1975/compendia/hist_stats_colonial-1970/hist_stats_colonial-1970p1-chD.pdf), reports labor-force participation by race from 1954 only, at 64.3 percent for "Negro and other races" against 58.2 percent for whites, and the gap stays in that direction through 1970. The BLS [Handbook of Labor Statistics 1975](https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/publications/bls/bls_1865_1975.pdf), Table 63, shows 1948 unemployment of 9.4 percent for nonwhite males aged 16 to 17 against 10.2 percent for white males the same age, and 1954 at 13.4 against 14.0. For males 18 to 19 and for teenage females the nonwhite rate was already higher in both years. No race breakdown for the censuses of 1890 to 1940 was read in this pass, so that part of his sentence rests on his text.
source: Walter E. Williams, "The Welfare State's Legacy," walterewilliams.com, September 20, 2017

prompt: How does "Discrimination and Liberty" define discrimination, and what does he treat as the test of a commitment to choice?

choices.text: Discrimination means only government action. A private choice is not discrimination.
Discrimination is the act of choice. The test is whether you allow choices you find objectionable, not only choices you approve.
Any income gap between two groups is discrimination, and it is illegal.
Choosing a spouse or a university is the one kind of choice he says the law should ban.

explain: He defines discrimination as choice, then applies the word to picking a university or a mate as well as an employee. The test he states is permission for choices the speaker dislikes. [Discrimination and Liberty](https://fee.org/articles/discrimination-and-liberty/) calls those cases university discrimination and mate discrimination. He adds that choosing a PC “harms” the maker of Macs and that a preference for California wines “harms” Bordeaux manufacturers. He says people routinely discriminate by race in choosing a mate, that he has not heard calls for mandatory integration in marriage, and that this assortative mating has helped perpetuate large income and wealth differences between blacks and whites. The test printed on the page is whether you permit choices you find objectionable, not only choices you deem right.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Discrimination and Liberty," FEE, April 1, 1998, https://fee.org/articles/discrimination-and-liberty/

prompt: A public library, paid for by taxes, wants to turn patrons away by race. What does "Discrimination and Liberty" say?

choices.text: A public board may exclude by race if it votes to do so.
Public libraries are private associations, so the essay leaves access aside.
Every citizen is entitled to access, whatever their physical attributes. Charging someone for the service and then denying it is the equivalent of theft.
Public schools may sort by race. Public libraries may not.

explain: He draws the line at government-financed services such as schools and libraries. If the public pays, every citizen is entitled to get in. He treats a racial bar there as immoral. [Discrimination and Liberty](https://fee.org/articles/discrimination-and-liberty/) calls schools and libraries the clearest case where racial discrimination has no place. If they are publicly financed, every citizen, regardless of physical attributes, is entitled to access. Requiring someone to pay for the service and then denying the benefit is, he writes, the equivalent of theft.
source: Walter E. Williams, "Discrimination and Liberty," FEE, April 1, 1998, https://fee.org/articles/discrimination-and-liberty/

prompt: What historical claim does "The Welfare State's Legacy" make about black family structure after slavery?

choices.text: The family was weaker in the first decades after emancipation than in the 2010s.
There is no evidence on family structure before 1965.

He cites a 1938 encyclopedia figure of 11 percent of black children born to unwed mothers, set against about 75 percent in his own time, and says the family was stronger in the first 100 years after slavery than in the second.
The 1938 figure he cites is 75 percent, and he treats that as a decline that began under slavery.

explain: The column's bottom line is that neither slavery nor Jim Crow nor the harshest racism has decimated the black family the way the welfare state has. The 11 percent and 75 percent figures are the comparison he uses for births to unwed mothers. Outside research. The column is [The Welfare State's Legacy](https://www.creators.com/read/walter-williams/09/17/the-welfare-states-legacy). NCHS puts births to unmarried non-Hispanic black mothers at 72.5 percent in 2010, [Births: Final Data for 2010](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr61/nvsr61_01.pdf), Table 15, and 69.8 percent in 2016, [Births: Final Data for 2016](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr67/nvsr67_01.pdf), Table 9. His "about 75 percent" sits above both. The 1938 encyclopedia figure of 11 percent was not found in print. The Census Bureau's [Vital Statistics of the United States, 1938](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/vsus/VSUS_1938_1.pdf), Table Q, reports 169.1 illegitimate births per 1,000 for "all other races," about 17 percent, in a registration area that left out four large states and, by the Bureau's own note, under-reported illegitimacy.
source: Walter E. Williams, "The Welfare State's Legacy," walterewilliams.com, September 20, 2017

prompt: How many books does his own biographical sketch say he wrote, and what does it say about Good Intentions?

choices.text: Three books. Good Intentions is the autobiography.
Ten books. The State Against Blacks was later made into the PBS documentary Good Intentions.
One book, the dissertation. Good Intentions is a novel by another writer.
Twenty books, all published by the Joint Economic Committee.

explain: The sketch says he authored ten books, lists them, and says The State Against Blacks was later made into the PBS documentary Good Intentions. The ten titles on that page are America: A Minority Viewpoint, The State Against Blacks, All It Takes Is Guts, South Africa's War Against Capitalism, Do the Right Thing: The People's Economist Speaks, More Liberty Means Less Government, Liberty vs. the Tyranny of Socialism, Up From The Projects: An Autobiography, Race and Economics: How Much Can Be Blamed On Discrimination?, and American Contempt for Liberty. George Mason's department tribute says 11 books, and the UCLA memorial's Wall Street Journal quotation says 13. The question follows his own sketch, which says ten. [Biographical sketch](http://walterewilliams.com/about/).
source: Walter E. Williams biographical sketch, walterewilliams.com, http://walterewilliams.com/about/

prompt: Which book is the autobiography, and which documentary does his sketch tie to it?

choices.text: The State Against Blacks is the autobiography, and Good Intentions is the 2014 film of it.
Up from the Projects, Hoover Institution Press, 2010, is the autobiography. The sketch says the PBS documentary Suffer No Fools is based on it.
Race and Economics is the autobiography. Suffer No Fools is a film about South Africa.
America: A Minority Viewpoint, 1982, is the autobiography, and he names no documentary.

explain: Up from the Projects is the autobiography. His sketch says Suffer No Fools, shown on PBS stations in 2014 and 2015, is based on that book. Good Intentions is the documentary he ties to The State Against Blacks, not to the autobiography. His publications list gives Up from the Projects: An Autobiography, Stanford: Hoover Institution Press, 2010. Hoover's book page is dated December 1, 2010, and describes lower-middle-class beginnings in a mixed but predominantly black neighborhood in West Philadelphia, two years in the army, a BA and graduate school at UCLA, and the George Mason appointment. The [sketch](http://walterewilliams.com/about/) is the page that ties Suffer No Fools, shown on PBS stations Fall/Spring 2014/2015, to that autobiography, and Good Intentions to The State Against Blacks.
source: Walter E. Williams biographical sketch, walterewilliams.com, http://walterewilliams.com/about/; publications list, same site, dates Up from the Projects to Hoover Institution Press, 2010, http://walterewilliams.com/publications/publications/

The Case for Reparations. McGraw-Hill, 1982.
A Novel of Philadelphia. Regnery, 1987.
Minutes of the Department. George Mason University, 2001.

prompt: Which of his real books is the 1995 Hoover collection subtitled The People's Economist Speaks?

choices.text: All It Takes Is Guts
South Africa's War Against Capitalism
Do the Right Thing
Liberty Versus the Tyranny of Socialism

South Africa's War Against Capitalism is the 1989 Praeger monograph. Liberty Versus the Tyranny of Socialism is a 2008 Hoover essay collection.
